case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       is ruled out already qualifies.

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.

Case:
A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.

Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

  B. Vaccine-associated measles
  C. Flare of rosacea
  D. Allergic reaction to vaccinations

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

[Clinical case]
A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10

case_info.scenario: A man in his 40s with a history of a matched, sibling allogeneic stem cell transplant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 7 years prior presented with a generalized eruption 1 week after receiving a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. The diffuse rash started as pink patches on the face (Figure 1A) and spread to the trunk and extremities within 4 days. Within a day of the MMR vaccination, he reported fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, loose stools, and dyspnea 7 days before the rash began. Pertinent negatives included no itch or pain associated with the rash and lack of any sclerotic skin changes.1He had received a COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna) 2 months prior, and along with MMR, an adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) 1 week prior. Following the patient’s stem cell transplant, he had relapsed disease 1 year later and was treated with donor lymphocyte infusion. Graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) complication of the mouth, eyes, liver, and lungs was treated with systemic steroids and tapered off. The most recent GVHD flare occurred 1 year prior to presentation, and the patient had not been undergoing immunosuppression for 6 months. The patient had also been treated intermittently in the past with oral minocycline for rosacea. Physical examination revealed an erythematous exanthematous eruption with generalized distribution across the trunk, extremities, and face with erythematous erosions noted in the buccal mucosa of the oral cavity. Skin biopsies were performed from the upper right side of the back and right temple (Figure 1B). Further diagnostic testing involved chest radiograph and laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and an infectious workup.
case_info.caption: A, Exanthematous eruption of pink papules on the patient’s face. Similar presentation seen distributed generally across the trunk and extremities. B, Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400. Folliculosebaceous epithelium depicting scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and rare syncytial-type multinucleated epithelial cells (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated overlapping features of cutaneous GVHD and cutaneous manifestations of measles. Within the interfollicular and follicular epidermis, there was basovacuolar change with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes and satellite cell necrosis, most consistent with either GVHD or measles. Within the folliculosebaceous epithelium (Figure 1B), rare syncytial-type multinucleated cells were seen, also consistent with measles infection.2,3Nasopharyngeal and urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for measles. IgM enzyme immunoassay results were positive and IgG enzyme immunoassay results were equivocal. Laboratory results showed complete blood cell count within normal limits and elevated creatinine, aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, ferritin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Chest radiography portrayed perihilar fullness only. The infectious workup showed positive results for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgA receptor-binding domain. The patient’s eruption and symptoms resolved with supportive care alone, without any immunosuppression. No contacts developed any symptoms. Measles is a contagious, airborne viral disease typically presenting with an exanthem after systemic and respiratory symptoms, eg, fever, myalgias, and cough.2,4It is preventable through a 2-dose MMR vaccine series.2,4Adverse events are generally mild with rare serious effects typically in immunocompromised patients.4Within known cases of vaccine-associated measles, presentation includes an acute, generalized eruption, without known distinctive clinical features to distinguish from wild-type measles, which can be differentiated with genotype and PCR. Vaccine-associated measles is exceedingly rare; in cases identified thus far,4there are no known reports of viral transmission. This patient had a history of GVHD and presented with a diffuse rash and systemic symptoms. GVHD management typically involves immunosuppression slowly tapered as tolerated.5During the tapering process, patients may experience GVHD flares,6which may include skin manifestations. Common cutaneous manifestations of chronic GVHD include poikilodermatous, lichenoid, and sclerotic features.7Other common features of GVHD, not sufficient for diagnosis, include erythema, pruritus, and a maculopapular rash involving areas such as ears, face, palms, and soles. After transplant, acute GVHD eruptions may prove difficult to distinguish from viral infections, which can mimic GVHD clinically and may present with interface dermatitis histopathologically (Figure 2). In this case, erythema and a facial maculopapular rash were observed, but this was not definitive for a GVHD diagnosis. Given this case’s systemic symptoms and cutaneous involvement, it proved challenging to completely exclude a concomitant GVHD flare. PCR test positivity for measles 2 weeks after MMR vaccination and resolution without intervention strongly support measles infection. Although the patient had a history of rosacea, pathology and clinical context did not support that diagnosis. An allergic reaction to MMR was not likely given the positive PCR and biopsy results. We suggest that this case represents a rare case of vaccine-induced measles. As typical GVHD management causes immunosuppression, careful consideration must be taken when administering vaccinations. Current recommendations are to continue with nonlive vaccinations such as influenza, especially given the potential of serious infections with immunosuppression.8However, vaccinations may be postponed based on immunosuppression dosage administered, timeline of treatment, and current status of GVHD.5Current recommendations are to avoid live-attenuated vaccines in patients with active GVHD.9In this case, current recommendations would point toward postponing vaccinations, especially live-attenuating, until control of chronic GVHD has been maintained without immunosuppression for a significant duration, even more than 2 years.10
